headline: Fake job ads recruit foreigners for Russia's army

sources.title: Russia's military recruitment networks exploit Western tech platforms (ISS Today, Institute for Security Studies)
Russia: Trafficking of Foreign Nationals to Fight in Ukraine (Amnesty International)
Politico: Western platforms are helping Russia recruit foreigners to fight in the war against Ukraine (LIGA.net)

chunks.text: On October 6, 2026, a South African research institute wrote about a new [[investigation]] into Russian army recruiting. It was done by Code for Africa, an African group of [[investigators]]. They found 289 websites, [[social media profiles]] and other online tools. Many were {{set up}} in Russia and Belarus but [[hosted]] on Western computers. The recruiters mostly {{go after}} young men without [[steady work]] in Africa and other [[lower-income]] regions.

verbs.correct: To create something, such as a website
verbs.wrong: To keep something to use later
verbs.why: Many people set up small online stores from home. Scammers often set up fake websites in a few hours. Many of the recruiting websites were set up in Russia and Belarus.

verbs.correct: To choose someone as a target
verbs.why: Some phone scams go after older people. That company goes after college students with its ads. The recruiters mostly go after young men without steady work in Africa and other lower-income regions.

chunks.text: According to the investigators, the ads look like [[ordinary]] job offers. They promise construction work, jobs as [[security guards]], visa help or film roles. Some websites carry [[forged endorsements]], such as the logos of Western news outlets. Politico reported that one ad promised 15,000 dollars for {{signing up}} and 3,000 dollars a month. When people {{fill out}} the online forms, their [[personal details]] are sent to Russia.

verbs.correct: To agree to join the army
verbs.wrong: To end a message or a letter
verbs.why: Many young people sign up for the army after high school. Fewer students sign up for the military each year. One ad promised 15,000 dollars for signing up and 3,000 dollars a month.

verbs.correct: To write answers on a form
verbs.wrong: To do someone's job for a while
verbs.why: Patients fill out a form at the front desk. Most job seekers fill out many applications each week. When people fill out the online forms, their personal details are sent to Russia.

chunks.text: In a report on September 10, 2026, Amnesty International said Russia has recruited thousands of people from low-income countries. Many were promised [[civilian]] jobs or Russian [[citizenship]] but {{ended up}} on the [[front line]] in Ukraine. Amnesty spoke with 15 foreign [[prisoners of war]]. Only three said they knowingly signed a military contract. A South African truck driver applied for a driving job in Poland, his wife said. He {{found out}} in Moscow that he would become a soldier. Amnesty says these practices [[amount to]] [[human trafficking]] in many cases.

verbs.correct: To finally be in a place you did not plan
verbs.wrong: To visit a place for a short time
verbs.why: Travelers who take the wrong bus often end up downtown. Many art students end up working in banks. Many recruits were promised civilian jobs but ended up on the front line in Ukraine.

verbs.correct: To learn a fact you did not know
verbs.wrong: To solve a problem by thinking
verbs.why: Most people find out about parties from friends. Workers often find out about job changes by email. The truck driver found out in Moscow that he would become a soldier.

chunks.text: Tech companies have {{taken down}} some of the content. Code for Africa's director said Meta has removed more than 300 [[ad campaigns]]. But new sites quickly {{pop up}}, the investigators say. Google [[disputed]] some of the findings and said it is {{looking into}} the report. The researchers say [[billing records]] could help {{track down}} the people behind the ads. Media reports suggest more than 3,000 Africans have {{gotten caught up in}} the war.

verbs.correct: To remove something from a website
verbs.wrong: To check whether a site is safe
verbs.why: Schools take down photos from their websites when parents complain. Many people take down angry posts an hour later. Tech companies have taken down some of the recruiting content.

verbs.wrong: To stop working for a while
verbs.why: New coffee shops pop up on our street every year. Strange messages often pop up on my screen. The investigators say new recruiting sites quickly pop up again.

verbs.wrong: To ask a company to pay a fine
verbs.why: A good manager looks into every customer complaint. Police look into the cause of every big fire. A Google representative said the company is looking into the report.

verbs.correct: To find someone after a long search
verbs.why: Police usually track down hit-and-run drivers in a few days. Some people track down old friends on social media. The researchers say billing records could help track down the people behind the ads.

verbs.wrong: To be paid well for a job in another country
verbs.why: Many people get caught up in their friends' arguments. Young fans sometimes get caught up in fights after a game. Media reports suggest more than 3,000 Africans have gotten caught up in the war.

mainIdea.s: Researchers say a network is using fake job ads to bring poor men from Africa and elsewhere into Russia's army. A rights group says many were tricked and may be victims of trafficking.
mainIdea.why: Investigators found hundreds of websites and profiles used to recruit men. Amnesty International says many recruits ended up on the front line after promises of civilian jobs.

mainIdea.s: A new study says Western tech firms have agreed to help Russia find soldiers across Africa. Meta and Google are now sharing their files with the police so the recruiters can be found.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the networks break the platforms' own rules. Google disputed some findings, and researchers only say billing records could help track down the recruiters.

mainIdea.s: African leaders met in Kenya to discuss how many of their students are moving to Russia for college. They hope new exchange programs will help young people find better jobs at home.
mainIdea.why: This is about fake job ads that recruit foreign men for Russia's army. Amnesty International says many recruits ended up on the front line.

tf.s: Many recruiting websites were set up in Russia and Belarus.
tf.why: The researchers found that many of the sites came from Russia and Belarus, but they were hosted on Western computers.

tf.s: The recruiting ads only offer jobs in construction.
tf.why: They also promise jobs as security guards, visa help or film roles. Recruiters use them to go after young men without steady work.

tf.s: Many foreign recruits ended up on the front line after promises of civilian jobs.
tf.why: Amnesty said many were promised civilian jobs or Russian citizenship. Most of the prisoners it spoke with did not knowingly sign a military contract.

tf.s: Amnesty said the recruiting has nothing to do with human trafficking.
tf.why: Amnesty says these practices amount to human trafficking in many cases. Many people found out too late that they would become soldiers.

tf.s: Meta has taken down more than 300 recruiting ad campaigns.
tf.why: Code for Africa's director said Meta removed them. But new recruiting sites quickly pop up again.

tf.s: Google agreed with every finding in the report.
tf.why: A Google representative disputed some of the findings. He said the company is looking into the report.

lines.text: Did you see the story about fake job ads for Russia's army?
No. What kind of fake ads?
They look like ordinary offers. Construction work, security jobs, even roles in a film.
Basically. Investigators found 289 websites and profiles. Many were {{set up}} in Russia and Belarus.
Who are they trying to reach?
They mostly {{go after}} young men in Africa and other poorer regions who need steady work.
And when someone {{fills out}} a form, what happens?
Their personal details are sent to Russia. One ad promised 15,000 dollars just for {{signing up}}.
That's a lot of money if you don't have a job.
Amnesty International says many men {{ended up}} on the front line. One truck driver thought he had a job in Poland.
He was flown to Moscow. That's where he {{found out}} he would be a soldier.
Who's running all this [[behind the scenes]]?
Nobody knows for sure. The researchers say billing records could help {{track down}} the people behind the ads.
Have the tech companies done anything?

Meta has {{taken down}} hundreds of campaigns, but new sites {{pop up}} fast. Reports say more than 3,000 Africans have {{gotten caught up in}} the war, and that may be just [[the tip of the iceberg]].
So if you're looking for work abroad, you really have to [[do your homework]] and be [[on the lookout]] for fake offers.
